entries.title: He Won the Nobel Prize for Protein Design. Now He Uses AI to Create Molecules Not Found in Nature
entries.summary: David Baker spoke with WIRED en Español about where biological design is headed next and the great potential and risks of taking biology outside the bounds of the natural world.
entries.content:
The natural world as we know it represents only a fraction of what might exist. Based on this idea, AI BioDesign was born: a scientific project that combines artificial intelligence and large-scale laboratory experiments to design and test new molecules and biological functions that are not found in nature but are physically and chemically possible.

In doing so, the researchers are aiming to create databases, models, and tools that could serve as “seeds” for developing the medicines and technologies of the future. The authors envision, for example, new drugs to treat cancer and neurodegenerative diseases or enzymes capable of breaking down plastics in the ocean.

The initiative is led by the Allen Institute, a biomedical research nonprofit in Seattle, along with the University of Washington and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center. Among the scientists leading the charge is David Baker, who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work in computational protein design.

For much of the history of biology, scientists have studied the solutions forged by billions of years of evolution. Exploring possibilities that nature never produced is a fundamentally new approach. And as technology makes this now possible, one that a leaders of the field even compares the potential of these methods to historic transformations such as industrialization, electrification, and the digital revolution.

However, delving into completely novel regions of biology also inevitably leads to difficult questions. WIRED en Español spoke with David Baker, chief scientific officer at AI BioDesign, to address this and other topics.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JORGE GARAY: AI BioDesign seeks to explore possible molecules and biological functions that have never existed in nature. Are there any particular risks involved in venturing into this uncharted territory? How can scientists anticipate those risks and what steps can they take to minimize them before a designed molecule leaves the lab?

DAVID BAKER: What’s exciting about biology is that nature has explored only a fraction of what is physically and chemically possible, which opens a world of possibilities for what we could design. When we explore those possibilities, the primary risks are not much different than those associated with any new biological technology—unintended interactions with living systems, unexpected environmental effects, or misuse.

The advantage we have today is that computational design allows us to evaluate many of these risks before a molecule is ever synthesized. We can screen designs computationally, test them extensively in contained laboratory settings, and subject them to increasingly realistic experimental validation before considering any real-world application.

The project mentions possibilities ranging from new drugs to plastic-degrading enzymes and even biological computers. If we have greater predictive power when designing new molecules and biological functions, how far do you think this capability could take us?

My team and I have lofty goals for protein design: We’re working to build a world where a cure for a new disease is created in weeks, not decades. Where our air, water, and soil are clean because we removed pollutants and reimagined the processes that contaminated them. Where crops thrive in conditions that once killed them. Where molecular machines pull critical minerals from waste and repair the infrastructure we depend on.

Proteins are the molecular machines life has developed to create all organic matter we know of here on Earth. Unlocking their full potential requires that we derive engineering principles that make it possible for innovative new ideas, including ones we can’t yet imagine, to be achievable.

As these models become more capable, could AI eventually design functional molecules that scientists themselves do not fully understand? If so, would it be enough to experimentally demonstrate that they work and are safe, or do you think we also need to understand the mechanisms?

Science has often progressed in stages, and we see that mirrored in how machine learning has advanced protein design. The first step is usually observing that something works, and we often only later understand why. Machine learning is really good at that first stage—it has vastly improved our capability to observe patterns that can be leveraged for biological design. Strong experimental evidence can justify moving forward with projects, but deeper understanding remains an important objective both for our research and scientific inquiry overall. Much of what we cannot achieve today is due to a lack of understanding or data that defines the parameters for how specific systems work or do not. This is the crux of the AI BioDesign program.

Are there molecules or biological functions that, in your opinion, should not be designed, even if it were technically possible to do so? What criteria should determine where that line is drawn?

Decisions should be guided by a balance of potential benefits and potential harms. Applications that address major challenges in health, sustainability, or human well-being have a strong case for development. Conversely, designs that create significant risks to public safety, security, or the environment deserve heightened scrutiny and, in some cases, clear restrictions.

Just as we have developed frameworks for other powerful technologies, we need governance structures that evolve alongside advances in AI and biotechnology. I’ve advocated that those restrictions should include monitoring and logging all synthetic DNA that is manufactured to record the sequence and its creator. This creates a practical barrier to misuse and a record of any ill-intentioned attempts.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: The Leftist Split Over AI Doom
entries.summary: The left wants AI regulation. They just can't agree on what it should look like or how concerned they should be.
entries.content:
On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.

The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”

As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.

Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.

“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Deng, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”

But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.

“The same people concerned about frontier governance and the development of superintelligence are also addressing those current harms,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI issues. “We should address all these other important factors. Those frontier AI abilities are true and increasing in power. They are not fake or hype.”

Over the past year, Sanders dove head-first into the world of AI safety, bringing conversations that were previously happening in Bay Area circles to Washington and his large populist base. The 85-year-old was early to both opposing data centers—a massive organizing pole for the left this year—and speaking out about AI’s potential harms, from job loss to existential dangers. His data center moratorium bill, released in March, explicitly linked pausing construction with the need to pass federal regulation to protect “the future of humanity.”

Sanders’s positioning on this issue has put him in some unusual alliances, most notably with Steve Bannon, President Donald Trump’s former adviser and a right-wing populist podcast host. It has also seemingly inspired a raft of messaging from left-wing candidates running for office across the country, many of whom have been tying broader concerns around AI to the furor over data centers. On September 9, a day before the New York DSA post, six candidates affiliated with the Working Families Party, including four backed by Sanders, released statements on the need for Washington to regulate AI to prevent existential threats to humanity.

This has come with both public and private criticism. AI researcher and tech industry critic Timnit Gebru has accused Sanders and others on the left of “taking their cues from literal doomsday eugenicist cults,” referring to the effective altruist and rationalist philosophies, which underpin AI safety conversations in Silicon Valley. And Sanders’s moves have inspired some private agita within certain left-wing circles.

“Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?” one NYC DSA member with a tech background tells WIRED.

Rumman Chowdhury, CEO and founder of the nonprofit Humane Intelligence, understands the concerns expressed by the DSA working group. Chowdhury, who formerly led the machine learning ethics, transparency, and accountability team at Twitter, thinks that all the attention that the AI safety discourse is generating will ultimately be beneficial to frontier labs.

“[The companies] grab all the attention, time, energy, and money by spouting really extreme perspectives. But then they actually backtrack to where we sit, all while they discount all of our expertise,” she says. “I think it's hard for normal people to think of how the mind of a venture capitalist works and these investors work. The scarier and more fantastic these CEOs make these companies seem, the more investors want in on it.”

For AI companies—particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, which aim to go public in the coming years—the attention and scrutiny on their products now could also be a boon in the long run. “Part of IPOing is sharing a lot of diligence documentation on risks and how risks have been addressed,” says Chowdhury. “This way, they can say, there is a full regulatory regime that they are part of establishing in this industry to guard against the worst risks, and that we have all established exactly what the ‘worst risks’ are.”

Pragathi Barusubramanian is a member of the NYC DSA’s Tech Action working group and a leader in the group’s anti-data center organizing, which netted a major win earlier this year by helping New York pass a one-year moratorium. Barusubramanian feels there may be a disconnect in the conversation around what exactly constitutes the most pressing AI-related harms to regulate. “When it comes down to what's happening on the ground,” they say, the conversation about existential risk “doesn’t come up at all.” Instead, they say, “there's an understanding that AI and data center companies don't have our interests at heart.”

McCoy, who is advising several Congressional candidates on AI, asserts that there is no real divide between actual leaders on the left on the issue. McCoy noted that several members of the DSA, including New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, have come out with recent statements about Coxon’s warnings and the Hugging Face hack.

McCoy says Gebru and similarly-minded critics are “marginal, unrepresentative, and also, frankly, picking an unnecessary distinction. It’s yes and. We should address harms like surveillance and Flock cameras, and other important factors. These do not come in any way at the expense of governing frontier AI capabilities.”

Phil Aroneanu, executive director of Irreplaceable, a left-leaning pro-AI safety organization, says that his time working as a climate activist has informed his approach to the AI regulation question. He believes that addressing both AI’s immediate and existing harms as well as future threats is both needed and possible. (McCoy helped found Irreplaceable with an initial seed fund from the Center for AI Safety.)

“This very similar intersection between the direct impact of fossil fuel extraction, people's homes getting flooded out because of climate-change-fueled storms, and then the broader movement focusing on the longer-term issue of risks and emissions,” he says.

Sanders and New York representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez don’t appear to be on the exact same page, either. While she cosponsored Sanders’ data center moratorium legislation, including the language around AI threatening humanity in her own House version of the bill, she has not participated in the high-profile AI safety discussions that he has been present for. While Sanders has called AI “the most transformational technology in the history of the world,” much of Ocasio-Cortez’s language around AI thus far has focused on data centers and the harms to jobs the technology could create, and worries that the industry is creating a bubble.

When asked by a reporter about AI safety last week, Ocasio-Cortez threaded a careful line, saying that “two things can be true at once,” noting AI “can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails,” and warning that “we could be seeing an economic bubble collide with a technological frontier.”

As the safety conversation quickly coalesces in Washington and in statehouses around the country, the ultimate question for the left is not whether to support AI regulation, but what regulations the movement should put its time and resources behind. Dang told WIRED that the DSA Tech Working Group supports “comprehensive AI and tech regulation at the federal, state, and city level, addressing frontier model regulation while also fighting back against the ways that corporate AI is already being used.”

A convention resolution currently before the DSA, meanwhile, proposes organizational support for Sanders and representative Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence altogether—hardly something the frontier labs would agree on. And any ideological concerns within the DSA itself may not matter too much when voters get a say. A Politico poll released Wednesday shows that two in three Americans think that there is at least some risk that AI could “destroy humanity.”

Barusubramanian says that, if nothing else, they’re “happy that everyone is talking about AI now.”

entries.title: Mophie’s Extendable MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand Is 50 Percent Off
entries.summary: Charge your trio of Apple gadgets–iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods–with one of my favorite telescopic stands.
entries.content:
Charging all your gadgets is an unavoidable daily task, but wireless charging makes it easy. Mophie’s uniquely extendable stand is one of the best Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers I have tested. And it’s available at a deep discount right now at half off (technically it’s 49 percent off). While this 3-in-1 stand has been discounted before, I’ve never seen it this low.

A 3-in-1 MagSafe charging stand is the best way to keep your desk or nightstand clutter-free but still charge your gadgets every day. This Mophie MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand has a pad for regular AirPods or wireless earbuds on the weighted base and an Apple Watch charger branching off. But this stand also features a clever trick: You can adjust the height of the iPhone charging pad.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Mophie

MagSafe 3-in-1 Extendable Wireless Charging Stand

Whether you have a low nightstand or work at a standing desk, this clever, compact stand enables you to keep your iPhone in your eye line. You can also turn your phone to landscape orientation for StandBy mode to use your iPhone as a bedside alarm clock. The 15-watt iPhone charger sits atop a telescoping pole that can extend from 7.5 to 16 inches. The pad can also tilt to your preferred angle. For content creators or folks making video calls, it can also serve as a tripod to help you film a quick video or take video calls.

The Mophie MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand is both MFi and Qi-certified to provide up to 15 watts to your iPhone. It can also deliver 5 watts to your Apple Watch and 5 watts to your wireless charging AirPods case or other wireless earbuds. You get a 36-watt power supply and a 5-foot USB-C cable in the box.

If you have issues with the height of your iPhone, this is the 3-in-1 stand you need. Height adjustment is not a feature I’ve ever seen in another charger, but you can find plenty of fixed-height alternatives in my best MagSafe chargers guide.

entries.title: It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
entries.summary: Heat records are being shattered thanks to a boost from the natural climate pattern—and burning fossil fuels, of course.
entries.content:
A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.

The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.

Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.

Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.

The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.

Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.

The heat hasn’t relented, despite the calendar turning to September. Even areas that typically escape countrywide heat waves have suffered. Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.

Why Has Fall Started So Hot?

Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US. Rising average temperatures raise the baseline for extreme heat, making very hot days even steamier now than they would’ve been just a few decades ago.

That trend has been especially notable at night: Many communities across the country have also seen a precipitous increase in overnight temperatures during the warm months as both temperatures and mugginess increase. The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.

A warmer climate is also altering upper-level patterns in a way that’s more favorable to extreme heat events. Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal. These ridges, often called heat domes, are more common in a warming world.

When Will the Heat End?

While overall highs for the remainder of September won’t be as extreme as they are in July, many areas will continue to endure summer-like heat.

El Niño is also lurking in the background. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters in the Pacific Ocean affects weather patterns around the world.

We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months as these abnormally warm ocean temperatures alter the jet stream, which are responsible for weather patterns during the autumn and winter months.

This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event. Each El Niño is different, but the patterns during previous strong El Niños suggest that a vast swath of the US is in for overall warmer-than-normal temperatures through the fall and winter. In other words, we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year.

entries.title: Napster Is Back, and It Wants to Digitally Clone Teachers
entries.summary: Once the music industry’s biggest headache, Napster’s next act is bringing AI to the classroom.
entries.content:
Napster is back. The name that struck fear into the hearts of music executives in the early dotcom era may be coming to a classroom near you.

In Dubai, United Arab Emirates, it has signed a strategic partnership with Gems Education to build AI agents and digital personas for education. In doing so, the once-notorious music-sharing company is bringing its technology into the classroom and testing how AI can augment the work of both teachers and students.

Today’s Napster, of course, bears no resemblance to its original incarnation as a peer-to-peer music-file-sharing service. Launched in 1999 by Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker, the platform revolutionized how people downloaded music, forcing the entire entertainment industry to rethink how content was distributed, sold, and controlled.

Napster eventually became the subject of a string of legal battles over copyright infringement and, following a series of adverse court rulings, had to shut down its original service in 2001.

Following its shuttering, the company went through various iterations, most recently as a music-streaming platform, until it was purchased by the Florida-based tech company Infinite Reality in 2025 for $207 million and pivoted to become an artificial intelligence platform. In January this year, it abruptly shut down its music-streaming service.

The company is now establishing a regional hub in Dubai, with Samuel Huber, formerly the founder and CEO of UK-based technology company Landvault—itself acquired by Infinite Reality in 2024—taking the helm as Napster’s CEO for the Middle East and Africa.

“The name has always been about giving power to the users,” says Huber. “Twenty-five years ago, it was about music and how music should be owned by people, not the gatekeepers. And now this is the same fight, the same ethos, but it’s about data and intelligence.”

Huber says that means challenging the power of the big AI companies. “The AI model companies have a lot of power; they’re building incredible models, and we want Napster to be an alternative to that.”

Napster’s work for Gems will develop proof-of-concept projects and showcases, including digitalising instructors, gamified learning, AI-assisted content creation, and classroom simulations.

The first phase will be anchored at the Gems School of Research and Innovation, where the Gems Global Education AI Hub and Gems Intelligence 360 platform will provide a real-world environment for educators, students, and partners to codesign, test, and evaluate AI agents and digital personas.

Napster will provide dedicated design, development, and product management resources based on Napster Learn, its AI-powered learning system. Digital twins of teachers, for example, will provide around-the-clock support.

Trained on a teacher’s material, courses, and papers, these digital twins will live online, becoming a “copy of yourself that you can then use to scale your time.” Students will be able to talk to them outside class, ask questions, refine concepts, and learn at their own pace, while teachers receive insights into the questions students are asking and where they may need additional support.

“We’re creating a better experience using voice, using video, to create a better way to interact with AI to make it more natural, so AI becomes more like coworkers rather than a machine or tool that you prompt, and we apply this technology in different verticals.”

According to Huber, AI agents and digital personas extend what teachers can do without replacing the human relationship at the heart of education. He also says student data will remain within the country and, where required, can be hosted on a company’s own servers. He also says Napster does not use user data to train its AI models.

While reassuring, much of this may well scare teachers fearful of losing their jobs. Although AI has caused considerable upheaval across multiple industries, Huber argues that its use in education should be about augmentation rather than replacement.

“I think it’s absolutely critical for educators, for professors, and for students to learn how to use AI in the right way. Because you’re right, there are two paths. We could let AI replace us. But if you’re using it in a smart way, you’re bringing insights, and then you use AI to augment yourself, just like you use word processors to type faster; then AI becomes a tool that augments you, not replaces you. I think students have that choice as well.”

The question is whether students and teachers actually want this and whether AI avatars can deliver meaningful educational benefits rather than simply offering a more sophisticated chatbot. In response, Huber says Gems will help Napster understand what students actually want from the technology.

“We’re not at the point yet where AI can fully replace humans, and therefore we want to leverage that technology overlaid on top of humans to get the most of it. What we’re building here is not about replacing the course, the lesson, the primary interaction between teachers and students that still happens in the real world.

“I think every student and every professor would want to support their students better,” he adds. "They would want to do one-on-one discussions with 200 students if they could, but there’s just no time. You can’t scale yourself this way.”

Napster’s move into the region is, in large part, driven by the UAE’s ambitious plans for AI. In May, the UAE Cabinet approved a federal framework for implementing agentic AI across ministries and government entities, supporting a plan to transition 50 percent of government services and operations to agentic AI models within two years. Napster wants to be part of that push.

Its partnership with Kameha Ventures, a Dubai-based venture platform led by Sheikh Ahmed Bin Mana Bin Khalifa Saeed Al Maktoum, is intended to help it tap into that market, bridging the gap between global AI capability and local deployment. Kameha will provide regional market development and institutional support, with localization of Napster’s offering a key priority.

“Localising the offering here is probably more important than in any other part of the world. Here, there’s a lot of cultural nuances that really matter, and even in digital products.”

Napster is also investing in local AI infrastructure. It has partnered with G42 in the UAE to host its data and run AI models locally, says Huber. In Saudi Arabia, it has collaborated with Lenovo and data center operator Detasad to run its infrastructure in-country, part of what Napster’s regional CEO describes as a broader push towards AI and data sovereignty.

Napster also plans to grow its roughly 20-strong regional team to about 500 by 2030.

“I’m here because there is a vision for AI in this country, which I find incredibly motivating and exciting as an entrepreneur, and we want to be one of the companies that help make that vision a reality. So we’re investing a lot in the country to make that happen.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED Middle East.

entries.title: Best Open Earbuds (2026): Shokz, Bose, Soundcore, and More
entries.summary: I’ve tested dozens of open earbuds. My favorite ones let you hear the world and your tunes equally.
entries.content:
Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.

I've tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.

For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Open Earbuds Overall

Specs

Connectivity Bluetooth 6.1
Battery life 10 hours, 40 with case
Water/dust resistance IP57
Wireless charging Yes

The Shokz OpenDots 2 are everything I want open earbuds to be. These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones. That's partly thanks to extremely long battery life—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and waterproof rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I've worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.

They're clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don't expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.

They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.

Runner-Up

Specs

Connectivity Bluetooth 5.4
Battery life 8 hours, 32 with case
Water/dust resistance IP55
Wireless charging No

Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata is a huge fan of the Soundcore Aeroclip for a lot of the same reasons I love the OpenDots 2. The Aeroclip buds are light, comfortable, and stable on your ear, plus they have stellar battery life and strong water and dust resistance (not waterproof). Waniata used them for daily life: walking the dog, strolling with the baby, riding bikes, making dinner, and hanging out at home—any situation where you want your music but also want to be aware or talk to people. The Soundcore app is easy to use and offers plenty of customization for controls, EQ, and multipoint pairing.

The brand recently announced the Soundcore Aeroclip 2 and Aeroclip 2 Pro, which I will be testing soon. Look out for deals on these original Aeroclips as a result.

Best Premium Open Earbuds

Specs

Connectivity Bluetooth 5.3
Battery life 7.5 hours, 27 with case
Water/dust resistance IPX4
Wireless charging No

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, they are still a solid, if expensive, option. That's mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds have a clearer, more defined sound than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.

Like the Shokz and Soundcore, they are supremely comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.

Best Cheap Open Earbuds

Specs

Connectivity Bluetooth 5.3
Battery life 7.5 hours, 30 with case
Water/dust resistance IPX5
Wireless charging No

It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren't totally convinced by. That's one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren't super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.

They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that's common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.

Best Open Ear Headphones

Specs

Connectivity Bluetooth 5.3
Battery life 12 hours
Water/dust resistance IP55
Wireless charging No

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more headphones than earbuds—they have a wraparound headband styling, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that's clearer than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.

I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I'm currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.

Honorable Mentions

Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn't clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that's forgivable.

JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.

Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested

EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.

Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.

Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.

Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.

What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?

At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.

Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.

When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?

Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.

What About Semi-Open Earbuds?

Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.

How Do I Test Open Earbuds?

I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.

With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

entries.title: Why AI Isn’t Likely to Wipe Out Humanity With Bioweapons
entries.summary: Of all the threats presented by uncontrollable artificial intelligence, scientists say death by plague ranks low.
entries.content:
Concerns about an AI-induced apocalypse are reaching a fever pitch, from Silicon Valley to Washington, DC.

One of the top theories about how a rogue AI will wipe us out? Biological weapons.

Earlier this summer, AI CEOs called for new laws to control the manufacturing of synthetic DNA. Then last month, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute showed that AI can design new viral genomes. The idea gained steam last week after Anthropic released a report indicating that there had been efforts to use Claude in ways that “could support biological weapons development. “The report authors cite biological misuse as “one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models.” Shortly thereafter, chief executive officer Dario Amodei urged the government to help AI labs “pace the frontier.”

Despite the alarm around an AI-created killer plague, many scientists say the risk is fairly low on the list of the world’s concerns.

David Bellamy, a research scientist at the Institute of Foundation Models in Sunnyvale, California, does not see AI as a fundamentally new threat when it comes to the creation of bioweapons. The scientific community has grappled for decades with the question of whether to publish potentially dangerous biological research—known as the dual-use dilemma.

Before large language models, the internet itself, open-access science journals, and translation services like Google Translate made it easier for people to access biological information, including lab protocols, Bellamy says.

“AI is essentially a tool that can help both good actors, like scientists, and also threat actors to peruse information more quickly and define and source those protocols more quickly,” he adds. “But those capabilities are not really the bottleneck in the production of bioweapons.”

The real bottleneck, he says, is the process of assembling a virus or other biological agent and the raw materials, equipment, and knowledge that would be needed to do so. A bad actor would need to obtain the necessary gene fragments and build a whole genome from scratch, then verify that the virus can infect humans, cause the desired illness, and be transmissible from person to person. Robotic lab assistants can automate some tasks and speed up workflows to a point, but a person would still need the know-how to run those experiments and the resources to carry them out.

Jason Kelly, the CEO of the biotech startup Ginkgo Bioworks, thinks it’s unlikely an artificial general intelligence could commandeer and disseminate existing pathogens, let alone engineer new ones and deploy them. Ginkgo Bioworks specializes in creating autonomous labs and recently ran a project with OpenAI where its GPT-5 model ran a lab.

“The AI could not take over the lab,” he says, in part because the humans who worked inside could simply decline to get the bot whatever substances and equipment it was requesting to physically produce a bioweapon. All those pesky humans acting as checks mean “you’d have to have dramatically more robots all over the place,” he says, for an AGI to be able to deploy machines to do the often-delicate virology work required.

Immunologist Derya Unutmaz likewise says humans would be able to thwart any attempts by AGI to develop a deadly disease. Even if a nefarious super intelligence did somehow manage to unleash a supervirus, he argues that scientists would be able to use other AI systems to swiftly develop a vaccine.

Still, even some people who don’t think that AGI independently siccing a bioweapon on us right now is a real threat are concerned about bad actors using the technology as well as what might happen down the line.

“It is impossible for AI to access a fully autonomous lab and autonomously build a virus today because fully autonomous labs do not exist yet,” says Olivia Scharfman, a biotechnology fellow at the technology think tank Institute for Progress. “But I do think that an AI could pay someone to do it for them.”

She thinks AI-assisted bioterrorism is an immediate threat and that there are some groups that might be nihilistic enough to do so, including “transhumanist AI successionists,” people who buy into a fringe ideology who hope to supplant humans with bots.

Other experts aren’t so worried about an AI bioweapon because they don’t think that biological warfare makes much sense methodologically. “The risks tend to be somewhat misunderstood,” genetic biologist and professor of computational biology Francois Belloux tells WIRED, noting that people tend to “overestimate the value of pathogens as weapons.”

Setting aside the AGI of it all, Belloux says that bioweapons are simply not an especially attractive choice for aspiring genocidaires, especially as it’s difficult to target certain groups and spare others, and mass-producing and distributing pathogens is logistically complicated versus, say, launching a bomb. “If you want to kill people, there are much, much, much better ways to kill them than to try to engineer some virus or bacterium and then release it,” he says—whether you’re the most sophisticated artificial mind ever created or just a regular human.

With AI bringing the threat of bioweapons into focus, Scharfman says this is the right moment to push for better protections against all biological threats, including existing pathogens like H1N1. That could include high-level actions like passing legislation to enhance security protocols around DNA synthesis technology, but she also advocates for changes to mitigate risk from all viruses, like upgrading air purification systems in buildings.

Whether AI demonstrably raises the risk of bioweapon development is a hard question to answer, says Steph Guerra, head of AI and bio at Rand Corporation, a policy think tank. “AI has been shown to be very good at integrating information together and being motivational to people for doing good and bad things,” she says.

Even if the risk is low, Guerra says, there are still ways that society can protect against potential misuse. One is that governments can adopt laws requiring firms that sell synthetic DNA and RNA to screen customers and orders to prevent the misuse of genetic material. Many companies already use software to screen orders for so-called “sequences of concern,” but the practice is not universal or mandated.

Before a bad actor could get to that point, though, most everyone agrees that models should have appropriate safeguards in place so that they don’t provide actionable, dangerous information to people.

Guerra says the risk of an AI-developed biothreat can also be mitigated by strengthening global surveillance systems to detect outbreaks of new diseases and circulating pathogens to researchers as early as possible. She says data-sharing protocols across AI companies, gene synthesis providers, and the government could also help prevent misuse.

“With pretty much almost any biosecurity control, there are going to be ways that they can be circumvented,” she says. “That's why we need layered approaches that provide friction across the entire pathway, from ideation to intention of a bad actor, all the way to the release of a bioweapon.”

Unutmaz says there’s an even more pressing worry: that all the AI doom conversations are diverting attention from how cutting-edge systems can assist humans in vaccine development and other medical breakthroughs.

“We really need to focus on the positive aspect of it,” he says.
